# Juan Fernando is now a researcher at the American Museum of Natural History

**Professor Juan Fernando Díaz Nieto was awarded the** _**honorary position of Research Associate**_ **by the American Museum of Natural History in New York (United States).**

**The academic teaches in the Department of Biological Sciences at EAFIT, and his research on taxonomy, morphology and DNA sequences in tropical mammals allowed him, in 2016, to discover new species of opossum.**

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias)
- [Our Impact](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/nuestro-impacto)
- Juan Fernando is now a researcher at the American Museum of Natural History

![Juan Fernando is now a researcher at the American Museum of Natural History.](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/70ecbb81-a76b-413b-a29e-c2c19e834d8b/web/juan-fernando.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=OqMacAZB)

As a research associate at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, Professor Juan Fernando Díaz will be able to open doors to future collaborations and more resources for research carried out by EAFIT students and teachers.

Many things happen in the course of a lifetime, and these take their place to form a story: a child may fall in love with the world while walking along the paths of the family farm; become interested in learning more about mammals; begin his university studies in biology; dedicate himself to teaching and research, and, at some point in the plot, be recognized with the _honorary position of Research Associate_ by the American Museum of Natural History, located in New York (United States).

This story, in particular, can be told by Juan Fernando Díaz Nieto, coordinator of the Biodiversity research group at EAFIT and professor in the Department of Biological Sciences at the institution, who received this distinction from the New York entity due to his advances in the knowledge of systematics (study to recognize the biotic diversity of the planet and its evolutionary relationships), and his collaborative work with researchers from the same.

For those working in the field of comparative biology, this position is, in Juan Fernando's words, highly prestigious, "as it is awarded to researchers with a significant contribution to the field of systematics. This position facilitates collaboration with the museum, both in terms of funding and logistics. During visits to the museum, I will be an active member of the research community and will receive special treatment regarding access to collections and resources."

Having access to more and better information translates into increased research output and the opportunity to publish academic articles in the museum's indexed journals, which enjoy enormous prestige worldwide. Furthermore, it will facilitate collaboration between the museum and EAFIT, since, through active collaboration with his counterparts in the United States, Juan Fernando can open doors to new research projects for faculty and students, as well as to more logistical and academic resources.

All of this stemmed from a relationship the professor began in 2008 with the American Museum of Natural History, after receiving a grant to visit several museums in the United States. “There I met Robert S. Voss, curator of mammals at that institution,” Juan Fernando recalls. “He is one of the foremost experts on mammal diversity in the American tropics, and we began an active discussion on the subject. Then, in 2009, I started my doctorate at the University of Minnesota, a period during which we worked very closely together.”

###### Passion for life

From childhood, Juan Fernando felt drawn to learning about biodiversity and exploring nature. He recounts how he would go out to explore the mountains and ravines of a family farm in Cundinamarca, and this experience helped him choose biology as his career path. At university, he dedicated himself to the rigorous study of mammals in Colombia, beginning his fieldwork and museum work to learn how to capture and analyze them. He also focused on expanding his knowledge of morphology, anatomy, and the characteristics necessary for species identification.

“For as long as I can remember, I’ve had a particular fondness for mammals. However, it wasn’t until I began my university studies that marsupials fascinated me. When I started fieldwork, I realized that many opossum species were extremely similar externally and that identifying them wasn’t easy. So I began the careful process of reading taxonomy articles, and I learned that the accurate identification of small mammal species is based on anatomical details that might seem minor.”

This allowed him to identify five species of opossums, two of them with some degree of threat of extinction, where it was believed that there was only one species with little relevance to the conservation of tropical fauna.

Valentina Grisales Betancur, a member of EAFIT's Biodiversity research group, highlights the professor's ability to ignite a love of research in his students, inspiring them with his approach to biology. "He lets us be both students and biologists," she affirms. "In fact, it was on his first field trip, in Anorí (Antioquia), that he saw a captured opossum up close for the first time and said that he had to study something so beautiful more closely, and the same thing happened to me later with bats."

The hours he spent in front of a microscope, observing mammal skulls and teeth, fueled his inquisitive spirit and thirst for knowledge, which he then shared with those who listened attentively in the classroom and followed him on field trips to various locations across Colombia. He considers his students at EAFIT to be innately passionate about biodiversity and dedicated to their studies.

And the feeling is reciprocal, according to what people like Mauricio Serna González, a Biology student at EAFIT and a member of the research group, say when asked about the teacher.

“He gives us all the foundation to be excellent biologists, and his interest is in training very good people in this field of knowledge, giving us the tools that allow us to stand out. He teaches as far as each person wants to go, and he is always willing to guide and support,” the student says.

###### Viruses versus bacteria: PhageLife's proposal for the swine sector from EAFIT

On a pig farm, a bacterial infection can jeopardize the animals' health and the farm's productivity. Furthermore, the problem becomes more complex when the bacteria stop responding to the antibiotics that previously combated them. To explore another approach, the company [PhageLife](https://phagelife.co/) is developing customized solutions using bacteriophages, naturally occurring viruses capable of eliminating specific bacteria.

metadata.description: En el término de una vida suceden muchos asuntos, y estos ocupan su lugar para ir formando una historia: un niño puede enamorarse del mundo mientras camina por los senderos de la finca familiar; interesarse por conocer más a fondo los mamíferos; iniciar sus estudios universitarios en biología; dedicarse a la docencia y la investigación, y, en algún momento de la trama, ser reconocido con la posición ad honórem de Research Associate (investigador asociado) por parte del Museo Americano de Historia Natural, ubicado en Nueva York (Estados Unidos).
